claim: `experimental: true` on a check page takes that check out of every phase on its own: `check/modules/checking/checking.module.code.ts:118` hands back no phases for it whatever the four `runsOn` flags say. The property means one thing, whether a check has landed and does not yet judge, and the mechanism lets it carry two: a check that never judged, and a check taken out of service. The page reads the same either way. `Alan Approves Checks` asks approval for adding a check and frees widening one, and says nothing about narrowing one to nothing; the page type's decision about switching a check on has no counterpart for switching one off. Eight of 66 checks state `experimental`, and not one of them ever judged. The only check ever taken out of service this way was put back the same day, so no instance is live now, and the audit command names all eight together as not yet judging.

evidence:
`check/modules/checking/checking.module.code.ts:118` is the whole mechanism: `judgingOn` hands back an empty phase list where `experimental` is true, and the four `runsOn` booleans it was handed are dropped. `check/modules/checking/checking.module.ts:30` states it as a decision, that a check whose page states `experimental` is gathered on no phase. So one optional property, required by none and absent from most check pages, takes a check out of change, worktree, deploy and audit at once. The four `runsOn` flags stay on the page and stay readable as intent while nothing consults them.

The one check ever in that state by a change rather than by never having judged was `module-sits-under-a-modules-folder`. Commit `646246f5568`, Aine <aine@alanwalton.com>, Sat Sep 12 08:23:59 2026 -0600, one file, four `runsOn` flags from true to false plus `experimental: true`. Its message says the modules-folder check is experimental and judges at no phase, and gives the reason: it ran at change over every module page, 6,672 module folders were not under a modules folder yet, and it refused any change to a page the nesting migration had not reached. At `runsOnChange: true` that left most of the repository unwritable, so the scale it answered was real. The flags went back the same day in `100671f6447`, Akasha, Sat Sep 12 20:17:11 2026 -0600, which judges at every phase again. The state lasted twelve hours, and no check is in it now. Nothing here is an objection to either change; those two messages are a good record, and they are the only record.

Eight of the 66 check pages state `experimental: true`, and not one of the eight ever judged. `folder-matches-a-shape`, `identifier-matches-its-place` and `decision-statement-is-plain` were born 2026-09-03 and marked by Thea on 2026-09-10, the day the property itself landed in `b519b9ba51e`, giving a check an `experimental` property saying the check has landed and does not yet judge. `folder-matches-a-shape` gained `runsOnAudit: true` in the very commit that marked it, so the marking raised its stated reach rather than lowering it. `no-unparsed-boundary-read` was marked the same day. `command-takes-its-arguments-through-one-reader`, `decision-restated-on-a-part-narrows-it`, `parts-list-is-sorted` and `no-unused-exports` were each born and marked on 2026-09-12. Not one of those eight judged and stopped, and with the modules-folder check judging again there is no live instance anywhere in the tree. That bounds the claim: the fault has happened once and has been undone.

`check/code/check-code.page-type.ts:177` carries the rule `Alan Approves Checks`, whose act at line 181 is to add a check to akasha only where Alan has approved that check, warranted because a check binds every writer on every change and a wrong one costs more than what it guards. Its four aids settle the neighbouring cases: approving the initiative is not approving a check, a check replacing an old one still needs approval, widening what an approved check reaches needs none, and how an approved check reads needs none. Every one of them runs in the adding direction. Taking an approved check out of service is not among them. The page type has weighed the on direction elsewhere too, at line 133, where an absence decision covers a change that switches a check on, so that the check does not judge the change that switched it on. There is no matching line for a change that switches one off.

The vocabulary has room for only one of the two states. `check/code/properties/experimental.boolean-property.ts:8` defines the property as whether a check has landed and does not yet judge. The page type says at line 125 that a check running on no phase has landed and does not yet judge, and at line 129 that the landing is how a check states its rule before that check binds anyone. Before, and not yet. A check that judged and stopped has no words of its own on the page.

Something does report it, in those same words and in one place. `command/pages/audit/audit.command.code.ts:82` builds a notice that an answer leaves out a count of checks not yet judging, naming each with the phases its page states. It runs at audit, and only where no check was named on the command line, so a change never meets it. While `646246f5568` was in force, because it set the four `runsOn` flags to false as well as setting `experimental`, `waitingOn` at line 76 found no stated phases for `module-sits-under-a-modules-folder` and printed it as a bare slug, while the checks that never judged printed theirs as waiting at change or at audit. In the one notice that told anyone any of this, the check that had been taken out of service was the entry that looked least like it was coming back.

What this informs rather than decides: whether taking an approved check out of service is Alan's the way adding one is. There is an argument that it should not be. The rule's warrant is the cost of a wrong check falling on every writer, and against that warrant the off direction is the safe one, which is why widening is free and narrowing goes unmentioned. The argument the other way is that an armed check guards something Alan approved, and the warrant weighs the cost of a wrong check without weighing the cost of a right one that stopped. If the answer is that it should be Alan's, the mend is one aid on `Alan Approves Checks` rather than any code, saying that taking an approved check out of service needs approval as adding it did. If the answer is that the reporting is the fault rather than the permission, a check could refuse a change that sets `experimental: true` on a check page that did not carry it before, which is a two-version comparison the change phase already holds the inputs for.
